opus-5.5.text:
I think there are a few reasons it's a natural place to start.

The first is that we're in a period of a lot of uncertainty. We don't yet know exactly which risks from frontier AI systems will turn out to matter most, or what the right technical thresholds are. If you try to write very prescriptive rules right now, like "your model must not do X," there's a real chance you get the details wrong, and then you're either stuck with rules that don't address the actual problems or rules that impose costs without much benefit. External audits are more flexible. They create a process where somebody independent looks at what's actually happening inside these systems and at the labs, and that process can adapt as our understanding improves.

The second reason is the information asymmetry. Right now the AI developers know vastly more about their models than anyone else: regulators, the public, even other researchers. Much of what we hear about safety comes from the companies grading their own homework. Even when people at those companies are acting in good faith, which I think many are, there are strong commercial incentives and competitive pressures that make it hard to be fully objective. An independent third party with real access can help close that gap, and the information they produce is what regulators need to make better rules later.

Third, there's a lot of precedent for this. In finance, aviation, and pharmaceuticals we don't just trust companies to say their products are safe; there's independent verification. Financial auditing in particular is a useful analogy. It's not perfect, but it established norms, professional standards, and liability around whether claims are actually true. Something similar for AI feels like a fairly modest, defensible ask, not some radical new idea, which makes it more politically achievable as a starting point.

And fourth, accountability changes behavior even before anything goes wrong. If labs know an external party will look at their evaluations, their internal safety processes, and how they handle dangerous capabilities, they'll take those things more seriously. It creates a baseline of rigor.

That said, I want to be clear that audits aren't sufficient on their own. An audit is only as good as the auditor's access, expertise, and independence. If auditors only get black-box API access, or can be shopped around for, or lack the technical skill to find the concerning behaviors, you get something closer to safety-washing than real assurance. So for this to work you need meaningful access, sometimes including model internals and training details; auditors with the right expertise; and eventually some teeth behind it, so that findings actually feed into decisions about whether and how a model gets deployed. But as a first step that builds the infrastructure and the knowledge we'll need for more serious regulation later, I think it's one of the most sensible things to push for.

r001.rationale: The response mentions uncertainty about risks and thresholds and says prescriptive rules could get details wrong, but does not say rapid AI advances may make thresholds obsolete before rules become law.

r002.rationale: It cites commercial incentives and competitive pressure as obstacles to objectivity, but does not identify good-faith reliance as vulnerable to adversarial gaming of regulation.

r003.rationale: It says external scrutiny can make labs take safety processes more seriously, but does not clearly describe an incentive for companies to explain their choices.

r004.rationale: It describes auditors examining evaluations, safety processes, and capabilities, but does not say audits let companies check whether their own choices are reasonable.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that we don't yet know what the right rules are. If you asked me today to write down the specific requirements that every frontier lab should have to meet, I could give you a list, but I'd have fairly low confidence that it's the right list, and I'd expect it to be outdated within a year or two. The technology is moving really fast, and our understanding of what makes a model dangerous or safe is still pretty immature.

So given that uncertainty, I think the question becomes: what's the thing you can do that's robustly good, that doesn't lock you into specific technical choices that might turn out to be wrong? And external audits and accountability mechanisms seem like a pretty strong answer to that.

The basic idea is: you don't necessarily have to tell labs exactly what to do, but you require them to let someone independent look at what they're doing, check whether their claims hold up, and report on that. Right now, almost all of the information about how safe these systems are comes from the developers themselves. They run the evaluations, they decide what to publish, they interpret the results. And even if everyone involved is well-intentioned, which I think they largely are, there are just structural incentives there. You're grading your own homework, you're under commercial pressure, you have deadlines. That's not a situation where I'd expect the public or governments to get an accurate picture.

So auditing does a couple of things. First, it creates an information flow to the outside world that isn't filtered by the lab. Second, it creates accountability, because if a lab says "we tested this model for dangerous capabilities and it's fine," there's now someone who can actually verify that or say, "actually, your methodology was weak here." And third, and I think this one is underrated, it builds institutional capacity. You get a body of people who are external to the labs but who actually understand the models, understand the evaluations, and can advise governments. Right now that expertise is very concentrated inside the companies.

The other thing I like about it is that it's somewhat analogous to how we've handled other high-stakes industries. In finance, aviation, pharmaceuticals, we didn't start by having regulators dictate every engineering decision. We built up oversight and reporting and independent verification, and then the more specific rules evolved from what we learned. I think AI is in that early stage, and auditing lets you learn while also putting some real checks in place.

I should say, I don't think it's sufficient on its own. Audits can be gamed, auditors can be captured, and if the model is really dangerous then knowing about it afterward isn't enough. So I see it as a foundation, something you build on, rather than the full answer. But as a starting point, it's one of the few things I think almost everyone across the spectrum of views on AI risk should be able to agree on.

r001.rationale: The response says the technology is moving fast and specific rules could become outdated, but it does not say regulatory thresholds may become obsolete before they become law.

r002.rationale: It describes structural incentives and commercial pressure even when developers are well-intentioned, but does not identify reliance on companies’ good faith as a vulnerability to adversarial gaming.

r003.rationale: It says audits can verify claims and report findings, but does not argue that external accountability gives companies an incentive to explain their choices.

r004.rationale: It describes independent auditors checking company claims and methods; it does not say audits let companies check whether their own choices are reasonable.

astra-6.text:
I think the basic problem is that AI companies know much more about their systems than either the public or the government does. And they also have incentives to deploy those systems quickly. So even if you think the people at these companies are well intentioned, you probably don’t want the whole regulatory framework to depend on them saying, “Trust us, we’ve checked this.”

External audits can help close that gap. An independent party can scrutinise the evidence behind a company’s safety claims: What did you test? What did you find? Are the safeguards actually effective? And where are you still uncertain? That doesn’t mean an auditor can certify that a model is safe in every possible circumstance. But it gives you a much stronger basis for making decisions than self-reporting alone.

And accountability is what makes that scrutiny matter. You need some way for findings to lead to changes, rather than just producing a report that everybody ignores.

I see this as a good starting point because you don’t have to know the perfect rule for every future AI system. You can build the institutions that let you understand what’s happening, challenge companies’ claims, and respond as the technology changes. It’s not the whole solution, but it’s a useful foundation.

r001.rationale: The response says institutions can respond as technology changes, but does not explain that rapid AI advances can make regulatory thresholds obsolete before they become law.

r002.rationale: It warns against relying on companies’ assurances, but does not identify good-faith reliance as vulnerable to adversarial gaming of regulation.

r003.rationale: It says accountability should make audit findings lead to changes, but does not argue that external accountability incentivizes companies to explain their choices.

r004.rationale: It describes independent auditors scrutinizing evidence behind safety claims, but does not say audits let companies check whether their own choices are reasonable.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one reason is that there’s a pretty big information asymmetry between the companies developing these systems and everyone else. The companies know much more about what they’re training, what the systems can do, and what problems they’re seeing. If you’re a regulator, it’s hard to make good decisions without some independent way to check those claims.

External audits can help with that. You can ask: Did you actually run the safety evaluations you said you would? Do those evaluations measure the risks we care about? And what happened when you found a problem? That gives you something concrete to hold companies accountable for, rather than just relying on their public commitments.

I also think it’s a useful starting point because there’s so much uncertainty. We don’t have to pretend we already know the right rule for every future AI system. We can start by creating mechanisms that make risks more visible and make it harder to ignore them, then improve the rules as we learn.

But the audit has to have teeth. If the auditor doesn’t get meaningful access, or if finding a serious problem has no consequences, then you can end up with a box-ticking exercise. The point is to create independent scrutiny that actually changes incentives.

r001.rationale: The response discusses uncertainty and improving rules over time, but does not say rapid AI advances can make regulatory thresholds obsolete before enactment.

r002.rationale: It notes information asymmetry and the need for independent checks, but does not identify reliance on companies’ good faith as vulnerable to adversarial gaming.

r003.rationale: It says audits support accountability and can change incentives, but does not argue that this gives companies an incentive to explain their choices.

r004.rationale: The audits described are independent scrutiny of company claims; the response does not present them as a way for companies to check whether their own choices are reasonable.
